strengths: Well-motivated approach leveraging structured reference materials to ground tool generation, addressing real limitations of pure LLM-based tool creation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct domains (causality, physics, chemistry) with multiple datasets and diverse baselines
Includes thorough ablation studies (Table 4) that meaningfully isolate contributions of code-form tool creation versus hierarchical selection
Practical efficiency gains demonstrated with cost analysis showing 97-99% reduction in inference time compared to iterative methods
Methodological rigor including tool validation, human evaluation of tool quality and consistency, and evaluation protocols
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution amounts to hierarchical organization of LLM-generated tools using standard techniques without substantial innovation
Narrow applicability and critical dependency on high-quality, structured reference materials and domain experts for validation, severely limiting generalizability

Modest and inconsistent performance improvements: headline '11.3% average' is misleading, with many comparisons showing only 1-3% gains; improvements larger against weak baselines (Creator) but smaller against stronger ones (PoT+ReAct)
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Creator is from authors' own prior work; ReAct baseline appears underfitted (46.3% average); missing comparisons with other retrieval-augmented reasoning methods
Limited human evaluation with only ~20 sampled questions per domain, no inter-annotator agreement, and no statistical significance testing for quality assessments
Arbitrary and unjustified hyperparameter choices (τc=1 chapter, τt=1 tool) with no sensitivity analysis or ablation
Weak analysis of failure cases: case studies are qualitative; no systematic error analysis or discussion of when/why RefTool fails
Overstated claims: abstract claims to 'overcome knowledge limitations' and provide 'generalized solutions' but results are highly domain-specific and modest in magnitude
Missing ablations on tool validation strategy, tool reusability across datasets, and reasoning model experiments relegated to footnotes showing only 4.3% improvement
Reproducibility concerns: no mention of code/data release, inconsistent technical details, key information in appendices

strengths: Well-motivated framework addressing genuine LLM limitations by leveraging structured external materials for tool creation
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three domains (causality, physics, chemistry) with multiple benchmarks, models, and both automatic and human evaluation
Strong and consistent results: 11.3% average improvement over existing methods, outperforming specialized domain-specific baselines
Systematic two-module design with clear hierarchical organization that naturally mirrors reference material structure
Human evaluation validates tool quality: ~90% faithful and useful tools, with good consistency between human and model selections
Significant practical efficiency gains: 97% inference time reduction and 99% cost reduction compared to specialized methods
Concrete case studies effectively demonstrate value of the approach on problems where baselines fail
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices with implementation details, prompts, evaluation protocols, and additional results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (LLM-based generation, hierarchical retrieval) without introducing fundamentally new methods
Scope restricted to knowledge-intensive quantitative reasoning tasks; unclear applicability to other domains like code generation or creative reasoning
Assumes access to well-structured reference materials; strategy for domains lacking such resources is not addressed
Requires LLMs to possess foundational domain knowledge for effective tool generation and selection; performance in unfamiliar domains unexplored
Hierarchical approach may not generalize to domains with different organizational structures than textbook-like hierarchies
Ablation study could be more comprehensive (e.g., sensitivity to prompt design, alternative hierarchical structures, different retrieval strategies)
Limited analysis of failure cases; paper focuses on successes with minimal discussion of when/why RefTool fails
Tool reusability claims demonstrated only on one additional dataset (SciBench-fund); broader generalization evidence would strengthen claims
Scalability with large reference materials not thoroughly analyzed; computational cost analysis limited to specific examples
Prompt engineering sensitivity not analyzed despite reliance on carefully designed prompts
Baseline comparisons with domain-specific methods may not be entirely fair; more comparisons with general tool-augmented reasoning methods would be informative

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach using external references to overcome LLM knowledge limitations, addressing a genuine gap in existing tool creation methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three knowledge-intensive domains (causality, physics, chemistry) with multiple datasets, baselines from four categories, and systematic generalization studies
Strong empirical results with consistent improvements: 13.0% over tool creation methods, 10.2% over domain-specific methods, with 99% cost reduction vs. ChemAgent
Thorough analysis including ablation studies (code format: 1.9%, hierarchical selection: 2.6%), human evaluation of tool quality (≥89% satisfactory), and cost-benefit analysis
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, comprehensive appendices with prompts and additional results, promise to release code and data
Tools are dataset-agnostic and reusable, with demonstrated compatibility across LLM families and successful generalization to non-scientific domains (language translation)
Clear technical soundness with logical two-stage pipeline (creation with validation, then hierarchical selection) and graceful degradation when no tools apply
weaknesses: Limited scope: only 3 textbooks across 3 scientific domains tested; textbooks are inherently well-structured, reducing evidence for messy/unstructured materials; XLR translation is sole non-scientific domain (single language pair)

Tool creation model dependency: GPT-4o achieves 82% direct validation success vs. 54% for Gemini-1.5-Pro; ~20% of weaker-model tools still filtered after refinement, raising concerns about knowledge coverage consistency

Hierarchical design not fully justified: two-level hierarchy appears arbitrary with no comparison of depth/structure alternatives; only 2.6% improvement over similarity-based retrieval is modest; LLM-constructed hierarchies for unstructured references lack quality validation
Potential data leakage: explicitly excluded one chemistry sub-dataset due to overlap with reference material, but no systematic verification that other evaluation questions don't align with textbooks

Incomplete failure analysis: human-model consistency ranges 44-90% for tool selection (especially weak in physics/chemistry) with limited investigation of failure modes; no systematic study of question types or domains where tools don't help

Tool validation limitations: relies solely on model-generated examples without verification of representativeness; pseudo-code validation for language translation is less rigorous than actual execution
Hyperparameter tuning inconsistency: grid search only performed for chemistry (nc, nt); causality and physics use defaults, raising questions about potential improvements with domain-specific tuning

Baseline fairness concerns: RAG subsection-level retrieval may not be optimal for text comparison; domain-specific baseline issues attributed to implementation rather than fundamental limitations; missing comparisons with recent 2024-2025 retrieval-augmented methods

strengths: Clear practical motivation and comprehensive experimental evaluation across three scientific domains with multiple LLM models
Strong reproducibility: detailed implementation details, complete prompt templates, and promised code release
Consistent empirical improvements (13.0% over tool creation methods, 10.2% over domain-specific methods) with thorough ablations and human evaluation
Demonstrates practical efficiency gains (97-99% reduction in cost vs. ChemAgent) and good generalizability within domains
Extensive analysis including tool quality assessment, case studies, and human consistency evaluation
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: components (code generation, hierarchical organization, verification) are straightforward; contribution is primarily combining known techniques rather than methodological innovation

Circular experimental setup: domain-specific textbooks are matched to domain-specific benchmarks (causal textbook for causal questions, physics textbook for physics, etc.), making improvements less surprising and more circular
Unfair baseline comparisons: RAG uses raw text while RefTool uses optimized code format; no comparison with more sophisticated RAG variants or fair optimization effort on both sides
Hierarchical selection not convincingly necessary: only 2.6% improvement over similarity-based retrieval (Table 4), failing to justify added architectural complexity
Generalization claims overstated: within-domain generalization is expected; cross-domain tool transfer untested; XLR translation is single cherry-picked non-scientific example
Insufficient failure analysis: no systematic error analysis, failure modes not examined, or how tool quality issues (4-11% problematic in Table 6) compound during reasoning
Hyperparameter choices not well-justified: 2 tools per section, default nc=1 nt=1 appear arbitrary; grid search only on chemistry creates methodological inconsistency
Limited generalization scope: all three domains are well-covered by standard textbooks; effectiveness on frontier/emerging domains untested; truly novel domain generalization unclear

strengths: Clear problem formulation with genuine motivation: addresses the real limitation that LLMs lack internal knowledge for specialized domains
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 scientific domains (causality, physics, chemistry) and 4 diverse LLMs with multiple benchmark datasets
Thorough ablation studies isolating individual contributions: code format (~1.9%) and hierarchical selection (~2.6%)
Strong analysis components: human evaluation of tool quality (≥89% satisfaction), cost analysis (97-99% efficiency gains vs. baselines), consistency with human experts, and case studies
Technically sound and reproducible: clear pipeline design, detailed implementation details, promised code/data release, comprehensive prompts
Consistent improvements across domains: 13% over prior tool creation methods, 10.2% over domain-specific methods, demonstrates generalization to non-scientific domains
Practical value: tools are reusable across datasets/models, significant efficiency gains (REFTOOL: 3-5 min vs ChemAgent: 20+ hours), works with unstructured references
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core components (tool generation via LLMs, hierarchical organization, validation) are not novel; primary contribution is reference-grounding, which is somewhat incremental over Creator, LATM, TroVE

Unclear contribution attribution: critical question unanswered—how much improvement comes from reference material vs. method design? Fine-tuning baseline (Table 8) achieves 46.0% vs REFTOOL 46.6% (marginal). RAG baseline underperforms but ablation doesn't isolate why

Tool validation rigor concerns: validation uses only single examples per tool (extremely limited); 13% of tools discarded after refinement; validation examples sometimes from reference (distribution mismatch possible); human evaluation on only 50 samples per domain

Reference material dependency unexplored: success appears highly dependent on reference quality/alignment; no systematic sensitivity analysis; references carefully matched to domains (somewhat cherry-picked); unclear if method works with misaligned but relevant references
Model dependency undermines reusability claims: Gemini/Llama-created tools have 54-48% vs GPT-4o's 82% direct validation success; tools appear model-specific; limits claimed reproducibility advantage

Moderate improvements in absolute terms: while '13% over prior methods' sounds significant, many improvements are 3-7% over strong baselines; inconsistent gains across models (GPT-4o: 6-8%, Llama: 3-5%); chemistry shows REFTOOL underperforms ChemAgent (57.7% vs 58.9%); no error bars or confidence intervals provided

Tool selection mechanism is simple and inconsistently effective: hierarchical selection consistency with humans varies dramatically (causality 94% vs physics 44-69%, chemistry 40-90%); insufficient analysis of why; similarity-based baseline performs comparably (Table 4), questioning hierarchical advantage

Limited failure mode analysis: insufficient discussion of when REFTOOL fails, which question types underperform, when external grounding doesn't help; no analysis of reference material variations on performance; Figure 6 shows indirect tool help but frequency unexplored

Scalability and generalization limitations: only 2-level hierarchy (adequacy for complex domains unexplored); evaluated only on technical knowledge domains; no evaluation on commonsense reasoning, creative tasks, or other types; generalization to XLR translation uses different methodology (pseudo-code) weakening claims

Statistical rigor gaps: significance testing claimed but no error bars, confidence intervals, or per-dataset significance testing; high variance in chemistry sub-dataset results (36-81% across conditions); aggregate statistics may mask high variance
